section_1_unit_metadata.essay_title: Introduction: Being-Moved: The Pathos of Heidegger's Rhetorical Ontology
section_1_unit_metadata.sub_unit_label: Opening + I (Hermeneutics or Rhetoric?) + II (Physis, Polis, and Heidegger's Style) + III (Heidegger the Humanist?)
section_1_unit_metadata.author: Daniel M. Gross
section_1_unit_metadata.notes_pages: (notes 1-49 are at book pp. 41-45; analyzed in HR-01-GROSS-B)
section_1_unit_metadata.essay_thesis_one_sentence: Heidegger's Marburg appropriation of Aristotelian rhetoric (especially in SS 1924, GA 18) — read against the Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft distinction, the antihumanist debate over middle voice, and the Gadamerian displacement of rhetoric by hermeneutics — discloses a 'rhetorical ontology' in which pathos is not a cynical addition to logos but the very ground of social being, such that rhetoric belongs at the heart of fundamental ontology rather than as an Aristotelian afterthought.
section_1_unit_metadata.thesis_in_gross_register: Heidegger relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology; the rhetorical genealogy of Being and Time's signature terms (Mitsein/koinonia, Glaube/doxa, Lage/being-in, Sorge, Stimmung/pathos, Augenblick/kairos, ekstasis, Angst/phobos, logos, Entschluss/krisis) has been lost with the displacement from rhetoric to hermeneutics, and recovering that genealogy requires reading SS 1924 as a formative moment, not a digression.

opening_no_heading.epigraph: Martin Heidegger, SS 1924 (English + German parallel): 'Tradition has long ago lost an understanding of rhetoric... Rhetoric is nothing less than the discipline in which the self-elaboration of Dasein is expressly executed. Rhetoric is no less than the elaboration of Dasein in its concreteness, the hermeneutic of Dasein itself.' [Die Rhetorik ist nichts anderes als die Auslegung des konkreten Daseins, die Hermeneutik des Daseins selbst.] (note 1: GA 18, p.110)
bullets: Frames the 'Heidegger and rhetoric' question as a story 'not yet adequately told' (p.1) despite Heidegger's epigraphic conviction.

Identifies a *double source* of modern rhetorical theory: Nietzsche's 1872 course *History of Greek Eloquence* and Heidegger's SS 1924 'Aristoteles: Rhetorik II' (per Lowith's transcript title) — these jointly mark 'the emergence of modern discourse theory' (p.2, n.4).

Stakes the volume's central historiographical claim: 'SS 1924 can be seen as a formative moment in Heidegger's lifelong project of grounding metaphysics' (p.2), citing Kisiel for the 'direct *genetic* link' between SS 1924 and *Being and Time*.

Lists ten *Being and Time* terms whose 'rhetorical genealogy' the book will trace: *Mitsein/koinonia*, *Glaube/doxa*, *Lage/being-in*, *Sorge*/care, *Stimmung/pathos*, *Augenblick/kairos*, *ekstasis*, *Angst/phobos*, *logos*/articulation, *Entschluss/krisis* (p.2). This list is the volume's organizing manifest; cites BT 158 explicitly.

Articulates four substantive innovations Heidegger makes in the rhetorical tradition: (1) elocutio refigured as conceptuality via tropes-as-poetic-logos that mark 'the contours of contingency' (p.3, contra Nietzsche's 'originary trope' and contra Saussurean arbitrary signs); (2) language as discursive medium rooted in 'shared moods, human institutions, and the nonchronological history these institutions compose' (p.3), with Heidegger's later 'art of listening' reversing Cicero/Demosthenes-style 'art of speaking' (citing *Unterwegs zur Sprache*); (3) the rhetorical-ontological thesis proper — 'Heidegger thus relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology' (p.4, italicized, the volume's titular claim) — humans 'simultaneously agent and patient, mover and moved'; (4) pathos as *not* a 'cynical and crowd-pleasing addition to logos' but 'the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation' (p.4), with a theological-Augustinian-Lutheran genealogy.

Closes the opening by naming the SS 1924-influenced cohort — Gadamer, Arendt, Brocker, Marcuse, Tugendhat (p.5) — and previewing the chapter trajectory. Asks the rupture question that Section IV will answer: 'Why, finally, if so productive, does Heidegger drop rhetoric as the antidote to metaphysics? Why, in other words, do hermeneutics subsume rhetoric after 1924?' (p.5)

section_I_hermeneutics_or_rhetoric.heading: I. HERMENEUTICS OR RHETORIC?
section_I_hermeneutics_or_rhetoric.rhetorical_structure: Critique-by-amplification: Gross uses Gadamer's *Truth and Method* (and Arendt's *Human Condition*) as foils that simultaneously preserve and 'depoliticize' Heidegger's rhetorical insight.
bullets: Frames the displacement of rhetoric by hermeneutics as 'a political and ethical loss' that is 'not absolute' but real (p.5). Acknowledges that hermeneutics solidifies a 'formal and universal method' (gain) while rhetoric — 'practiced in ad hoc fashion as a proactive art' — recedes (loss).

Reads *Truth and Method* through Klaus Dockhorn's 1966 review in *Gottingische Gelehrte Anzeigen* 218 (n.8, n.9), which Gross credits with prompting Gadamer's 'rhetorical' second-edition revisions; signals that Gadamer 'downplays the political loss' and that one must trace 'how the priority of pathos was depoliticized with the turn to hermeneutics' (p.6).

Reconstructs Gadamer's genealogy via Vico (n.14, p.7) and the Roman Stoic *sensus communis* — practical knowledge as *phronesis*, 'manifest above all in the Aristotelian triad of politics, ethics, and rhetoric' (p.7); but Gadamer emptied this through Kantian intellectualization (n.15) until Dilthey returned it via historicism (Heidegger's 'fresh beginning,' p.7, n.16).

Critique of Gadamer (load-bearing): in claiming that 'understanding' precedes 'affect' (citing *T&M* p.8, n.18), Gadamer 'cedes ground... to the very rationalists [Habermas, n.18, leading the charge] he sets out to criticize.' Gadamer 'chooses not to reclaim for rhetoric the doctrine of affections (*Affektenlehre*) as taught by the likes of Luther or Schleiermacher' (p.8, n.19). For Heidegger by contrast, 'pathos provides the very ground for critical judgement (*krisis*)' (p.9, n.23).

Tests Heidegger-Arendt link: Dana Villa's claim that Arendt 'spatializes' the authentic-inauthentic distinction (Arendt as appropriator, Heidegger as 'lonely venue of uncanny works and poetic words,' n.25, n.26). Gross counters: 'SS 1924 proves Villa wrong'; the lectures show 'an original Being-with obfuscated by *Being and Time* and practically invisible in Heidegger's later work' (p.10), and Arendt's 'speech' is for all intents 'Heideggerian/Aristotelian rhetoric' (citing *The Human Condition* on speech as 'the actualization of the human condition of plurality,' n.27).

Renders the section's positive thesis: 'each of these basic possibilities for meaningful speech [judicial and deliberative] reveals a political community: "Being-with." There can be no agent or patient, no speaker or hearer, unless one presumes a shared domain of past and potential meaning. And it is in Aristotle's *Rhetoric* that Being-with, *koinonia*, is given its definitive form' (p.11). Both Gadamer and Arendt left behind 'critical elements... the priority of pathos first among them.'

section_II_physis_polis_style.heading: II. PHYSIS, POLIS, AND HEIDEGGER'S STYLE
section_II_physis_polis_style.rhetorical_structure: Stylistic-philological exegesis. Gross builds a sustained close reading of GA 18 §§240-242 (with parallel German block-quote) to show that Heidegger's middle-voice German *style* is itself the philosophical instrument by which the *Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft* distinction is dissolved.
bullets: Sets up the contemporary scene: Aristotle's *Rhetoric* read 'alongside the Roman rhetorical works of Cicero and Quintilian' (p.11, n.30) and recently treated 'as a piece of philosophic inquiry, and judged by philosophic standards' (Garver, n.32). Heidegger 'preparing for this philosophical counter-thrust' citing GA 18.117: 'That we have the Aristotelian *Rhetoric* is better than if we had a philosophy of language' [Dass wir die aristotelische Rhetorik haben, ist besser, als wenn wir eine Sprachphilosophie hatten].

Heidegger's holistic reading: SS 1924 treats *Metaphysics, Politics, Nicomachean Ethics, Rhetoric, Topics, De anima, De motu animalium, Physics* in concert. *Pathos* 'a key term in the rhetorical tradition, provides the transfer point between social and naturo-physical phenomena' (p.12). This is the volume's most important methodological claim about why rhetoric is ontology.

*Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft* as foreign import to Aristotle: McKeon called the distinction 'sharp and unbreakable' but Heidegger 'takes such analogies seriously' (n.35), reads Aristotle holistically, and thereby 'relocates the long misplaced discipline of rhetoric.' Famous cosmological gloss: 'The pathos of a stone allows it to become part of a wall, the pathos of a plant to grow, the pathos of an animal to perceive imminent danger and to shriek a warning to others' (p.13). Human pathos is unique by *nous poietikos* — the faculty 'that allows us to extend into every domain of being and be moved even by things that are not there in body.'

Establishes the *Sein-in-Bewegung* thesis (the unit's title): 'Though only human being is moved to discourse, or *logos*, Being-moved is essential to all (*Sein-in-Bewegung*).' Cites GA 18.226 — pathos and *physikos* essentially bound; 'Being-moved... necessarily exceeds the rational psyche because people have bodies of a certain sort.' This grounds rhetoric in Aristotle's *Physics* III.

Critical aside on BT (p.13-14): 'Significantly, this aspect of Heidegger's philosophy drops out from 1927 — with political consequence.' BT 418 quotation on Dasein-as-not-substance-in-space; BT 420 quotation on situation-as-leeway. Gross frames this as a substantive *loss* in BT relative to SS 1924's discussion of 'special materiality of human Dasein.'

The middle-voice argument (the section's load-bearing move, pp.14-18): Gross gives a long bilingual quotation of GA 18 §§240-242 on *Miteinandersein* — German block followed by English — to display Heidegger's stylistic use of variations on *sein*, the prefix *be-* on *weg(en)*, the morphing of *bewegen* through *bewegt wird*, *Bewegung*, *Bewegen*, *Bewegendes*, and 'es gibt'-style impersonals. Argues that this stylistic experiment is *not* eccentricity but the only available means in German for what Greek can do in the middle voice: express 'simultaneity of being active and being passive, the nature of a life at the same time constructive and constructed.' Pivotal claim: 'these stylistic stutterings allow him to produce a discussion of *Miteinandersein* achievable by no other means' (p.18). Concludes the section by registering that this 'particular achievement... has been dramatically misunderstood' — setting up Section III's antihumanism critique.

section_III_heidegger_humanist.heading: III. HEIDEGGER THE HUMANIST?
section_III_heidegger_humanist.rhetorical_structure: Polemical mediation: Gross stakes a position between hyperbolic French antihumanism (Derrida, Foucault, Bourdieu, Pecora, Ferry-Renaut) and Habermasian liberal-Kantian critique. The section concludes with extended exegesis of Aristotle *Physics* 202b23 (kinesis) bridging into the rationale for the (forthcoming Section IV) priority-of-pathos argument.
bullets: Frames the antihumanist debate (pp.18-19): the 'middle voice' as locus classicus for both Heideggerian appropriation and Derridian appropriation (1968 *Margins of Philosophy* on *differance*; n.36). Lists the cohort: Derrida, Foucault, Bourdieu, de Man, Hillis Miller, Pecora, Ferry, Renaut. The shared but mistaken reading: 'Heidegger's discourse on language [as] the attempt to dissolve passion and action, subject and object.' Gross calls this 'a serious error.'

Reads Derrida's *differance* passage as exemplifying — via the French translation of *kinesis* / German *Bewegung*: *mouvance* — 'the modern middle voice,' but as misreading Heidegger by 'neutralizing' rather than 'relating' the active/passive interanimation. 'No more is resonance the act of being moved' (Derrida).

Engages Letter on Humanism (1946, p.19-20): generally read as 'the essential antihumanist text' and as foreshadowing Derrida's nontransitive subject. Gross resists: 'SS 1924 shows Heidegger to be at most the hyperbolic antihumanist's distant relative.' Cites Heidegger's claims that 'language is the house of Being' and that *ethos* means 'abode' or 'dwelling place' (Heraclitus Frag. 119) — not the dissolution of agency.

Engages Ferry-Renaut, Pecora's neoliberal critique (n.41): without agency, no neo-Kantian universal values, no human rights. Gross counters that SS 1924 'provides a description of humanity and ethical discourse that cannot be called in good faith either neo-Kantian or proto-Derridian. If anything, Heidegger's work in 1924 would be neo-Aristotelian and protocommunitarian. And it is in his middle voice discussion of the kinetic ambiguity of Being-in-the-world that Heidegger comes into his own' (p.20).

Builds the *kinesis* exegesis (pp.20-22): 'The key lies in the complex relationship between *pathesis* and *poietikos*, whose interanimation defines motion (*kinesis*) for Aristotle.' Gross gives Aristotle *Physics* 202b23 in three forms — Greek transliterated ('Kinesis: entelecheia tou dynamei poietikou kai pathetikou he toiouton'), Hardie/Gaye English ('Alteration is the fulfilment of the alterable as alterable'), and Heidegger's German rendering ('Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird,' GA 18.322). Argues: 'a definition need not describe a thing in terms of *genus* and *differentia specifica*... Heidegger makes the point emphatically and repeatedly that a thing that moves should not be determined in its Being according to the degree to which it participates (*methexis*) in motion, motion in turn understood as existing like a Platonic Idea beside the world of things human and natural. Instead *kinesis* should be understood as a fundamental way that Dasein *is*' (p.21, citing GA 18.288: 'Die kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst').

Returns to the late Heidegger essay 'Language' (1959, n.42): German middle voice via *es gibt* and *die Sprache spricht*. Compares to GA 18.108 'Rhetorike peithous demiourgos: Being able to speak makes possible the actual authority I have to persuade people — to determine how people are with one another' (parallel German). Argues: even as Being is 'no longer grounded in Dasein' in 1959 (post-*Kehre*), 'human being is in language and not the other way around, but passion and action, subject and object, agent and patient are there as constructed and interanimate terms' (p.23). Heidegger's 'middle voice in no way kills the author' — it 'describes in new terms how the author is rhetorically constituted.'

Closing (pp.24-27, with the *Aristotle physics* / *eidos of pathe* nexus): Gross returns to the Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft critique with the question 'What does a house look like?' (citing GA 18.205, GA 18.33). Heidegger as *rhetor poietikos*: 'A house appears in wood, stone and brick, so as to produce the necessary protection and shelter; it is a "being-built" carried out in light of a shelter being there.' Material is *realized* (*pathetikos*) and the realization takes place in *becoming concrete* (*poietikos*). 'The Being of nature as it presents itself to us is not determined solely in material, but rather in its Being-moved' (GA 18.205).

Closes Section III (book p.27) with the final move into pathe-as-eidos (preparing for IV: 'The Priority of Pathos'): 'The pathe indicate possible ways of being-moved that tie humans in a unique way to their embodiment.' Cites GA 18.206-207 in parallel German block: '*Affekte* sind nicht Zustande des Seelischen... Die Affekte spielen eine fundamentale Rolle bei der Bestimmung des Seins-in-der-Welt, des Seins mit und zu anderen.' Closes: 'Heidegger thus rearticulates a neglected moment in the rhetorical tradition in which pathos goes beyond a psychology of the autonomous subject. Aristotelian pathos, he argues in his unique phenomenological language, serves as the very foundation for *logos*, or social discourse.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: rhetorical ontology
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gross's titular term: the thesis that Heidegger 'relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology' (p.4). Not rhetoric as a sub-discipline within ontology but rhetoric as the discursive-existential medium in which fundamental ontology becomes possible. Operationalized through (a) tropes-as-contour-of-contingency, (b) language as discursive-historicized medium, (c) the human as agent-and-patient simultaneously, (d) pathos as ground of logos.

section_3_key_concepts.name: rhetorical genealogy of Being and Time
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The trail by which BT's signature concepts (Mitsein/koinonia, Glaube/doxa, Lage/being-in, Sorge, Stimmung/pathos, Augenblick/kairos, ekstasis, Angst/phobos, logos, Entschluss/krisis) descend from the rhetorical-Aristotelian apparatus of SS 1924 (pp.2, n.5-7). Gross treats the genealogy as 'lost' in BT itself and recoverable only by reading the 1924 lectures. Cites BT 158 as Heidegger's own admission of the connection.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Being-moved
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The titular concept (subtitle of essay): the kinetic-ontological condition shared by all beings — stones, plants, animals, humans — distinguished only at the human level by *nous poietikos* (intellect's power to extend into 'every domain of being'). Gross reads it as Heidegger's middle-voice rendering of Aristotle *Physics* 202b23 *kinesis*. Captures the 'simultaneity of being active and being passive, the nature of a life at the same time constructive and constructed' (p.17). The thesis 'pathos of a stone... pathos of a plant... pathos of an animal' (p.13) makes pathos cosmologically primary, with rhetoric as its human articulation.

section_3_key_concepts.name: pathos (as ground of logos)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The volume's master concept: 'the very condition for the possibility of rational discourse' (p.4). 'No cynical and crowd-pleasing addition to logos, pathos is the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation. Without affect our disembodied minds would have no heart, and no legs to stand on.' Gross treats pathos as cosmological (not just psychological): the pathe of a stone, plant, animal, human (p.13). For humans, pathos has a unique theological-rhetorical genealogy (Augustine -> Luther -> Heidegger 1924) treated in Section IV but introduced here.

section_3_key_concepts.name: middle voice
section_3_key_concepts.german_form: es gibt / die Sprache spricht / morphology of bewegen
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Greek-grammatical voice that expresses simultaneity of activity and passivity, neither active nor passive — the verbal form Heidegger reproduces stylistically in German (via *bewegen*'s morphological play, *be-weg-en* prefix-stem-suffix, the *es gibt* impersonal, and 1959's 'die Sprache spricht'). For Gross, *the* central stylistic-philosophical resource by which Heidegger operationalizes Being-moved. Distinguished from Derrida's *differance* / *mouvance* reading (which 'neutralizes' rather than 'interanimates' active/passive). 'Heidegger's middle voice in no way kills the author. Rather it describes in new terms how the author is rhetorically constituted' (p.24).

section_3_key_concepts.name: trope (as contour of contingency)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gross's revisionary account of Heidegger's *elocutio*-equivalent: 'a trope, acting in concert with its staid manifestation as a concept (*Begriff*), marks the contours of contingency' (p.3). Tropes 'provide the nontheoretical distance necessary to see how we are in our everyday situations and how we are moved.' Distinguished from Nietzsche's 'originary' tropes ('mobile army of metaphors,' n.3) and from rhetoric-as-ornament. The trope/concept dyad is constitutive, not decorative. Aligned with antihumanism without dissolving the speaking subject.

section_3_key_concepts.name: discourse (vs. communication)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's Marburg conception of language as 'rooted in shared moods, human institutions, and the nonchronological history these institutions compose' (p.3). Set against Saussurean 'arbitrary system of differences' and against communication-as-transparent-mind-meeting-mind. 'Following Foucault we tend now to call language so described "discourse." But SS 1924 demonstrates that Heidegger laid early tracks to a language part and parcel of human institutions and their histories' (p.4). Heidegger reverses Cicero/Demosthenes 'art of speaking' into 'art of listening' (citing *Unterwegs zur Sprache*).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Being-with-one-another
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotle's *koinonia* as Heidegger's *Mitsein*; 'it is in Aristotle's *Rhetoric* that Being-with, *koinonia*, is given its definitive form' (p.11). The political-rhetorical community presupposed by every speech act ('There can be no agent or patient, no speaker or hearer, unless one presumes a shared domain of past and potential meaning'). Gross emphasizes the *shared world* dimension via the GA 18 long quotation §§240-242: 'Miteinandersein ist zugleich: miteinander dieselbe Welt haben.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: deliberative rhetoric
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Gross's reading of GA 18: the genre that 'allows an advocate addressing a political assembly to characterize a problem, lay out concrete possibilities for future action, and forge a common opinion regarding what is to be done' (p.11, citing GA 18.124-125). 'Heidegger does extensively gloss what he calls the heart of the discipline: "deliberative" rhetoric.' Used to set up the Heidegger-Arendt link (Arendt's 'speech that allows humans to plan for the future and foresee the needs of those who will come after them').

section_3_key_concepts.name: epideictic / judicial rhetoric (background)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Mentioned briefly: 'The rhetoric of praise and blame, or *epideictic*, gets short shrift in Heidegger's course, as it does in Aristotle's text (see chapter 4 in this volume).' Judicial rhetoric ('the kind of speech that... provides a perspective on "what has happened"') invoked via Arendt and the example of sacrilege ('a sacred vessel is stolen from a private house').

section_3_key_concepts.name: physis / polis pairing
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Section II's titular pairing: Aristotle's claim that Being-in-the-polis has its 'foundation in the concepts of nature' (p.15, German block of GA 18.241). Against Socrates who 'put physis in the background when treating social phenomena,' Heidegger reads Aristotle as binding *physis* and *polis* essentially: 'we are there concretely for each other — simultaneously subject and object.' This grounds the dissolution of *Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft*.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Naturwissenschaft / Geisteswissenschaft distinction
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The post-Diltheyan partition Heidegger 'overextended' (Gross's word, p.24) by treating it as foreign to Aristotle. McKeon's defense ('sharp and unbreakable,' n.35) rejected. Heidegger's holistic reading collapses the distinction; the 'house question' (p.24-25, citing GA 18.205) shows materiality construed in terms of human-built realization, not Cartesian extension. *Geisteswissenschaft* and *Naturwissenschaft* are equally anachronistic to Aristotle.

section_3_key_concepts.name: phronesis
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian 'practical knowledge... directed towards the concrete situation' (p.7, n.14). Gross reads Vico-Gadamer-Heidegger as recoverers of phronesis against Cartesian-Kantian intellectualization. 'Manifest above all in the Aristotelian triad of politics, ethics, and rhetoric' (p.7). The 'recently reexamined domain of practical reason (*phronesis*), where rhetoric is purged of its sophistic ambiguities and reconstructed as a philosophy of everyday language' (p.12, n.34).

section_3_key_concepts.name: antihumanism (and its limits)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The reading associated with Derrida, Foucault, Bourdieu, Pecora, Ferry, Renaut, Lyotard, Lacan, Castoriadis, etc. — that Heidegger's middle voice 'dissolves passion and action, subject and object' (p.18). Gross calls it 'a serious error.' SS 1924 shows Heidegger to be 'at most the hyperbolic antihumanist's distant relative' (p.19). The polemical target of Section III; corrected by reading SS 1924 as 'neo-Aristotelian and protocommunitarian.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: humanism (Gadamerian sense)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Tradition Gadamer defends via Vico's *sensus communis* against Cartesian 'critical science'; the Italian-Roman 'practical knowledge' tradition treating social phenomena as not-random/not-perfectly-predictable but subject to *phronesis*. Gross uses 'humanism' ironically in a second sense (p.25): the 'humanist description' that defines a thing only by its *eidos*-as-appearance ('what is seen') — which Heidegger rejects in favor of construing things by their *being-built/being-moved* (the *rhetor poietikos* model).

section_3_key_concepts.name: rhetor poietikos (Heidegger as)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gross's coinage characterizing Heidegger's stylistic practice in SS 1924: 'realizing a body of Greek philosophical work in his unique language of phenomenology.' Operationalized in the 'house' passage (p.25): material is realized as it takes shape (*pathetikos*) and the realization 'takes place in becoming concrete (*poietikos*)' (citing GA 18.205). Aligns rhetorical-stylistic experimentation with ontological argumentation; Heidegger does philosophy by being a rhetor.

section_3_key_concepts.name: kinesis (as way of being of Dasein)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian *kinesis* (Physics 202b23) read by Heidegger as not Platonic-participatory but as 'a fundamental way that Dasein *is*' (p.21, GA 18.288: 'Die kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst'). The interanimation of *pathesis* and *poietikos* defines motion 'whose interanimation defines motion (*kinesis*) for Aristotle' (p.20). This passage 'reaches into the true center of the Greek view of the world and life.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: pathesis / poietikos (the kinesis dyad)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The complementary pair whose interanimation Aristotle uses to define motion: 'Kinesis: entelecheia tou dynamei poietikou kai pathetikou he toiouton' (Physics 202b23). Gross emphasizes that for Heidegger this pair is *not* a binary but an interanimation: the kinetic ambiguity that the German middle voice reproduces. 'Material is realized as it takes shape (*pathetikos*) and the realization takes place in becoming concrete (*poietikos*)' (p.25).

section_3_key_concepts.name: soma (as obtrusiveness)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Citing GA 18.28 in parallel German-English: 'When we translate *soma* with "body" we must be aware that for the Greeks *corporeality* did not mean materiality. *Soma* means instead a particular *obtrusiveness* of a being, a being-there... that belongs to me, stands immediately available to me, is there for me in its specific obtrusiveness and self-evidence.' Anti-Cartesian: rejects body-as-extension in favor of body-as-disclosed-availability.

section_3_key_concepts.name: eidos of pathe
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Closing concept of Section III (p.27, GA 18.206-207): 'The *eidos* of the *pathe* is a disposition toward other humans, a Being-in-the-world.' Pathos in the *Rhetoric* is treated 'with respect to *eidos*' rather than physiologically — Aristotle 'does not achieve the basic determination of a living thing from physiological considerations.' This sets up Section IV's full pathos-priority argument: pathe are *neither* purely psychological *nor* purely material/physiological but are dispositional ways-of-being-toward-others.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's SS 1924 lecture course (GA 18) is a *formative* moment for *Being and Time*, not a peripheral interpretive exercise — it provides the rhetorical genealogy for ten signature BT terms that BT itself partially conceals.
premises: Kisiel's reading: SS 1924 is 'one of Heidegger's greatest courses, breaking ground not merely in Greek philosophy but also for his entire path of thought' (n.6).

The list of BT key terms (Mitsein/koinonia, Glaube/doxa, Lage/being-in, Sorge, Stimmung/pathos, Augenblick/kairos, ekstasis, Angst/phobos, logos, Entschluss/krisis) reads 'like a glossary of key terms from Being and Time' (p.2).
BT 158 is Heidegger's own admission that his concernful-understanding-to-theory back-formation is traceable through Aristotle's Rhetoric.
targets: Conventional readings that treat SS 1924 as a digression from Heidegger's mature thought.
Pöggeler's restriction thesis (anticipated; addressed in HR-01-GROSS-B and at volume frame).
section_4_main_positions.pages: 1-2, citing BT 158 and GA 18 epigraph at p.1

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology — rhetoric is not a sub-discipline within ontology but the discursive-existential medium in which fundamental ontology becomes possible.
premises: Heidegger SS 1924 GA 18.110: 'Rhetoric is nothing less than the discipline in which the self-elaboration of Dasein is expressly executed... the hermeneutic of Dasein itself' (epigraph).
Humans are 'simultaneously agent and patient, mover and moved' (Aristotelian terminology, p.4).
The four substantive innovations (elocutio-as-tropology, language-as-discourse, agency-as-doubled, pathos-as-ground) compose 'the substance in which contemporary rhetorical theory moves' (p.3).
targets: The 'critique of Heidegger as a radical antihumanist and deconstructor of human agency' (p.4).

The 'epistemology of tropes popular during the Enlightenment (for example, Dumarsais and Fontanier)' and 'critique of ornamental style (Ramus and the Port Royalists through the eighteenth-century British Elocutionary movement).'
The romantic tradition of 'rhetorical invention as a matter of individual genius and passion as a matter of individual psychology.'

section_4_main_positions.claim: The displacement of rhetoric by hermeneutics — exemplified by Gadamer's *Truth and Method* — entails a 'political and ethical loss' that, while not absolute, is nonetheless real and that 'depoliticizes' the priority of pathos.
premises: Gadamer credits Dockhorn 1966 (n.8, n.9) with prompting *T&M*'s rhetorical second-edition revisions, but still 'downplays the political loss' (p.5).
Gadamer 'cedes ground... to the very rationalists [Habermas, n.18] he sets out to criticize' by claiming understanding-precedes-affect (p.8).
Gadamer 'chooses not to reclaim for rhetoric the doctrine of affections (*Affektenlehre*) as taught by the likes of Luther or Schleiermacher' (p.8).
Gadamer's pessimistic claim that 'in the age of the written word, communication no longer depends on the orator... and "carry the listener away"' (n.22) misses Heidegger's SS 1924 alternative.
targets: Gadamer's *T&M* account of the rhetoric-hermeneutics relation.
The Habermasian 'organizing a perfect and perfectly manipulated information' framing (citing Habermas n.18).
Christopher Fynsk's reading (n.24) of Gadamer/Ricoeur as obfuscating 'a more originary sense of hermeneutics.'

section_4_main_positions.claim: Hannah Arendt's political philosophy — long read as appropriating Heidegger's 'lonely' authentic-disclosure into a public agonistic space — is in fact already congruent with Marburg Heidegger's rhetorical-political reading, which Villa misreads.
premises: Villa's claim (n.25) that Arendt 'spatializes' authentic disclosure against Heidegger's 'venue of uncanny works and poetic words.'
SS 1924 reveals 'an original Being-with obfuscated by *Being and Time* and practically invisible in Heidegger's later work' (p.10) — precisely the Being-with Arendt operationalizes politically.
Arendt's 'speech is the actualization of the human condition of plurality' (*Human Condition*, n.27) corresponds to 'judicial rhetoric' (p.10) and 'deliberative rhetoric' (p.11) Heidegger glosses.
targets: Villa's reading of the Heidegger-Arendt relation.
The 'lonely Heidegger of poetic words' reading of authenticity.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Pathos is the ontological transfer point between social and naturo-physical phenomena, dissolving the *Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft* distinction Heidegger 'overextended.'
premises: GA 18 treats *Metaphysics, Politics, NE, Rhetoric, Topics, De anima, De motu animalium, Physics* holistically (p.12).
'The pathos of a stone... pathos of a plant... pathos of an animal... Unique to human pathos is a dependence on *nous poietikos*' (p.13).

Aristotle's basic ontology grounded in *Physics* categories (citing GA 18.226 / Physics 284): pathos and *physikos* essentially bound; 'these categories do not just ground individual beings as such, but also social being: *Miteinandersein*.'
Heidegger's holistic Aristotle-reading takes McKeon's 'sharp and unbreakable' distinction (n.35) seriously enough to invert it.
targets: McKeon's defense of the natural/human sciences distinction (n.35).
Dilthey-Husserl scientism that construes bodies as material substance (the 'house' question, p.24).

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's German-stylistic experiment with the middle voice (variations on *sein*, the *be-* prefix on *wegen*, the *bewegen-bewegt-Bewegung-Bewegen-Bewegendes* morphology) is *not* mere stylistic eccentricity but the philosophical instrument by which the simultaneity of activity and passivity in *Miteinandersein* becomes expressible in German.
premises: Greek middle voice expresses 'inherent multiplicity in the One' (p.17); German lacks this, so Heidegger reproduces it morphologically.
Long parallel quotation of GA 18 §§240-242 displays the stylistic operation.
'Heidegger's stylistic stutterings allow him to produce a discussion of *Miteinandersein* achievable by no other means' (p.18).
The stylistic operation has been 'dramatically misunderstood' (by both antihumanists and their critics).
targets: Conventional readings of Heidegger as stylistically opaque or merely difficult.
Antihumanist appropriations that read style as content-dissolution (Derrida via *mouvance*).

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's middle-voice work in 1924 is 'at most the hyperbolic antihumanist's distant relative' — neo-Aristotelian and protocommunitarian rather than proto-Derridian — and the standard reading of *differance* / *Letter on Humanism* / *die Sprache spricht* as Heidegger-extending antihumanism is a serious error.
premises: Derrida's *Margins* (1968, n.36) reading of middle voice as 'cannot be conceived... as the action of a subject on an object' *neutralizes* what Heidegger interanimates.
Letter on Humanism's 'language is the house of Being' and *ethos* = 'abode/dwelling place' (Heraclitus Frag. 119) preserve, not dissolve, ethical agency (n.39, n.40).

Ferry-Renaut critique (n.38, n.41) of antihumanism's 'difficulty accommodating itself to the newly rediscovered reference to human rights' applies to Foucault/Bourdieu/Derrida-style readings *not* to SS 1924.
Pecora's (n.37) 'Ethics, Politics, and the Middle Voice' overreads a continuity between SS 1924 and 'apathetic' antihumanism.
targets: Derrida's *Margins of Philosophy* (1968) reading of middle voice (n.36).
Vincent Pecora's neoliberal critique of Heidegger's middle voice (n.37).
Ferry-Renaut's *French Philosophy of the Sixties* (n.38, n.41) when applied to Heidegger directly.
Foucault, Bourdieu, de Man, Hillis Miller as antihumanist appropriators.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Aristotle's *kinesis* (Physics 202b23) — 'the entelecheia of the alterable as alterable' — should be read, with Heidegger, as 'a fundamental way that Dasein *is*' rather than as Platonic participation in a separate Idea of motion; this anti-Platonic reading licenses Heidegger's whole project of binding *physis* and *polis*.
premises: Greek text: 'Kinesis: entelecheia tou dynamei poietikou kai pathetikou he toiouton' (Physics 202b23).
Hardie/Gaye English: 'Alteration is the fulfilment of the alterable as alterable' (or 'fulfillment of what can act and what can be acted on, as such').
Heidegger's German: 'Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird' (GA 18.322).
GA 18.288: 'Die kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst' ('motion is a mode of the Being of Dasein itself').
The anti-genus/differentia move: 'a definition need not describe a thing in terms of *genus* and *differentia specifica*' (p.21).
targets: Scholastic-Aristotelian reception that requires genus/differentia definition.
Platonic-participatory readings of *kinesis* as participation (*methexis*) in a separate Idea.

section_4_main_positions.claim: The late Heidegger's 'Language' essay (1959) 'die Sprache spricht' is *not* a deepening of antihumanism but a continuation of the SS 1924 rhetorical-ontological framework — even after the *Kehre*, 'human being is in language and not the other way around, but passion and action, subject and object, agent and patient are there as constructed and interanimate terms.'
premises: GA 18.108 'Rhetorike peithous demiourgos' — 'Being able to speak makes possible the actual authority I have to persuade people — to determine how people are with one another.'
The 1959 'Language' essay's *ent-sprechen* / *Unter-schied* coupling preserves the 'speech-as-rhetorical-disclosure' grammar of 1924.
Both passages reject (a) language-as-physiological-utterance and (b) language-as-tool-of-internal-thought-externalization.
targets: Readings of 1959 'die Sprache spricht' as antihumanist subject-effacement.
Periodization-rupture readings that sever pre- and post-Kehre Heidegger absolutely.

section_4_main_positions.claim: The *eidos* of the *pathe* is 'a disposition toward other humans, a Being-in-the-world' — Aristotle's pathe in the *Rhetoric* are not Stoic states-of-the-soul nor Ciceronian ancillary inflectors of cognition but ontological dispositional structures that ground rather than supplement *logos*.
premises: GA 18.206-207 (parallel German-English): '*Affekte* sind nicht Zustande des Seelischen, es handelt sich um eine *Befindlichkeit des Lebenden in seiner Welt*... Die Affekte spielen eine fundamentale Rolle bei der Bestimmung des Seins-in-der-Welt, des Seins mit und zu anderen.'
Heidegger's claim (BT-cited at p.27): the second book of Aristotle's *Rhetoric* 'must be taken as the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another.'

Pathe are 'neither merely psychological emotions... nor are they simply physical-material alterations ("boiling blood," or a "cold sweat"). Rather the pathe indicate possible ways of being-moved that tie humans in a unique way to their embodiment' (p.26).
targets: Stoic accounts of emotion as states of soul/psyche.
Ciceronian account of pathos as ancillary to rational discourse.
Modern psychology of autonomous-subject emotion.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Gross simultaneously claims (a) BT 158 cites Aristotle's Rhetoric as source of the concernful-understanding-to-theory dynamic AND (b) BT 'partially conceals' / 'drops out' the SS 1924 special-materiality discussion. Q: Is BT a faithful or unfaithful executor of the SS 1924 rhetorical genealogy?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.evidence_pages: 2 (BT 158 cited approvingly), 13-14 (BT 418/420 cited as drop-out), 27 (BT 178 cited approvingly)
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: Gross's position is nuanced: BT *acknowledges* the rhetorical source (158, 178) but the *substantive treatment* of materiality and middle voice present in GA 18 is muted. The tension is generative for Section IV's pathos genealogy. [INTERP-low: I read this as Gross's deliberate ambivalence rather than internal contradiction.]

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Gross sets Heidegger against Plato (Plato as 'villain,' p.23) but also notes that Plato becomes a Heideggerian villain only in WS 1924-25 (Plato: Sophistes), and that 'the ax falling on former favorites' is 'characteristic of his pedagogy at the time.' Q: Is the SS 1924 anti-Platonism a stable Heideggerian commitment or a pedagogical posture?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: [INTERP-low] This is signaled but not fully resolved by Gross; the resolution requires reading WS 1924-25 (GA 19), which is outside this unit.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Gross argues Heidegger's middle voice is *neither* simply active *nor* simply passive (P6) AND that it 'in no way kills the author' (P7). Yet the GA 18 §§240-242 passage explicitly distributes a single subject across an interior/exterior position pair. Q: Does the German morphological play actually preserve agency, or does it dissolve it into pre-individuated kinetic ambiguity?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: [INTERP-high] Gross's position would be that 'agency' in the SS 1924 register is neither Cartesian unitary subject nor postmodern dissolved subject but rhetorically constituted distributed-yet-real agency. He doesn't fully argue this; the move is asserted at p.24 as a thesis.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: P9 (1924/1959 continuity thesis) sits in tension with the section's repeated framing of post-1924 Heidegger as the figure who 'drops' rhetoric (p.5). Q: Is the late Heidegger (1959 'Language') continuous with SS 1924 (P9) or is rhetoric 'dropped' after 1924 (Section I framing)?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: Gross's resolution: rhetoric-as-named-discipline is dropped, but rhetoric-as-ontological-grammar persists. This is implicit; HR-01-GROSS-B presumably elaborates.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Gross's 'rhetoric central to fundamental ontology' (P2) directly contradicts Pöggeler's titular 'Heidegger's *Restricted* Conception of Rhetoric' (Ch 7). Both use SS 1924 as evidence. Q: How does the same GA 18 yield 'central' for Gross and 'restricted' for Pöggeler?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: This is the volume's master tension VT1 (per phase0-overview Section 7). Productive.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Gross treats Gadamer's T&M position as 'depoliticizing' (Section I throughout) but defers to Ch 2 for Gadamer's 'revised' position. Q: How much does Gadamer's interview revise the T&M reading Gross critiques here?

Gross uses the rhetor poietikos / Heidegger-as-rhetor framing (P6) — but Hyde (Ch 4) develops the call-of-conscience/epideictic framing more directly. Q: Are Gross's 'middle voice' Heidegger and Hyde's 'silent epideictic' Heidegger compatible figurations?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.evidence_pages: Section II throughout; bridge to Ch 4
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: [INTERP-low] On first reading these are compatible — Gross's rhetor poietikos is not specifically deliberative or epideictic, leaving room for Hyde's specification.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: GA 18.110 ('Rhetorik ist nichts anderes als die Auslegung des konkreten Daseins, die Hermeneutik des Daseins selbst') is BCAP unit U-FP3a's central passage. Gross uses it as epigraph; BCAP pipeline reads it ontologically. Both readings agree, but the BCAP pipeline frames the passage in fundamental-ontology terms while Gross frames it in *rhetorical-ontology* terms. Q: Are these compatible or rival framings?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.annotation: Compatible: rhetorical ontology is fundamental ontology approached through its discursive-existential medium. The framings are aspectual.

section_10_local_graph_edges.note: Gross's titular thesis: 'Heidegger thus relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology' (p.4 italicized). Rhetorical ontology IS fundamental ontology read through its discursive-existential medium.

Gross P10: 'pathos is the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation' (p.4) and 'the very condition for the possibility of rational discourse' (p.4). Logos presupposes (is grounded in) pathos.

Gross's titular concept: 'Sein-in-Bewegung' renders Aristotle's kinesis. GA 18.288: 'Die kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst' — kinesis is Dasein's mode of being.

Aristotle Physics 202b23: Kinesis is defined by the interanimation of pathetikos (passive-undergoing) and poietikos (active-making). Gross: 'whose interanimation defines motion (kinesis) for Aristotle' (p.20).

Gross P6: Heidegger's German morphological play (variations on bewegen) is the stylistic instrument that *operationalizes* the kinetic-ontological condition of Being-moved in a German that lacks the Greek middle voice. Style as philosophical method.

Gross via GA 18.241: 'Aristotle saw and shifted the weight of his work initially to the investigation of physis as Being. He thereby established the foundations for an investigation of Being as such... The concepts of Being-in-the-polis also have their foundation in the concepts of nature.' Gross's pathos-as-transfer-point thesis (P5) undermines the Diltheyan partition between natural and human sciences by showing pathos to be cosmologically primary (stones, plants, animals, humans).

Gross's claim that hermeneutics 'depoliticizes' rhetoric undermines Gadamer's T&M position that understanding precedes affect; the move 'cedes ground... to the very rationalists [Habermas] he sets out to criticize' (p.8).
Gross argues Derrida's differance/mouvance reading 'neutralizes' what Heidegger's middle voice 'interanimates' — a serious error per Section III.
Gross's centrality thesis is in direct titular opposition to Pöggeler's restriction thesis. Both cite GA 18 as evidence; the volume opens with A and closes with B.
Gross's reading of Arendt-Heidegger affinity via deliberative/judicial rhetoric *supports* and is supported by Kisiel's protopolitical reading of GA 18 (Ch 6). Cross-essay alignment.

Heidegger's identification of rhetoric with the hermeneutic of Dasein (GA 18.110) operationalizes Aristotle's pathe-analysis in Rhetoric II as a hermeneutic of everydayness. (Cross-link explicit at p.27 via BT 178.)

Heidegger's GA 18.288 ('Die kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst') refines Aristotle's Physics 202b23 kinesis-definition by reading it not Platonically (methexis) but as Dasein's mode of being.

BT 178's claim that Aristotle Rhetoric II is 'first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another' presupposes the SS 1924 GA 18.110 'Rhetorik ist nichts anderes als die Hermeneutik des Daseins selbst' identification.

Heidegger's 'house' passage at GA 18.205 exemplifies Aristotelian Physics II's nature/techne treatment by showing material as realized through being-built (skepasma) — material is shaped (pathetikos) and realization takes place in becoming concrete (poietikos).

Gross P-supporting: 'a trope, acting in concert with its staid manifestation as a concept (Begriff), marks the contours of contingency' (p.3). Tropes are how discourse acquires the depth that distinguishes it from arbitrary signs (Saussure) and from communication (Habermas).

Self-loop with note: pathos *shifts* its meaning across registers — psychological emotion (modern), state-of-soul (Stoic), ancillary-cognitive (Cicero), Befindlichkeit/eidos-of-pathe (Heidegger SS 1924). Gross argues the SS 1924 reading recovers an Aristotelian pathos-as-disposition that the intervening tradition obscured.

Gross's middle-voice-as-philosophical-instrument argument (P6) supports his rejection of antihumanist appropriations (P7): if the middle voice IS interanimation rather than dissolution, then Heidegger is at most antihumanism's 'distant relative.'

Dockhorn's 1966 review of T&M in Gottingische Gelehrte Anzeigen (n.8) is credited by Gross as catalyzing Gadamer's rhetorical second-edition revisions — Dockhorn refines Gadamer's hermeneutic project from a rhetorical direction.
Heidegger's reading of kinesis as Dasein's-mode-of-being (P8) undermines Platonic-participatory readings of motion as participation in a separate Idea (methexis). Plato as 'villain' (p.23).

P9 (1924/1959 continuity) complexifies P3 (rhetoric is dropped after 1924): rhetoric-as-named-discipline is dropped, but the rhetorical-ontological grammar (middle voice, agent/patient interanimation) persists into the late writings. The 'drop' is selective.

LOCUS-to-LOCUS edge: Aristotle's Physics III definition of kinesis (202b23) supports/grounds the pathe-analysis in Rhetoric II by giving the kinetic ontology in which pathe operate — 'pathos a key term in the rhetorical tradition, provides the transfer point between social and naturo-physical phenomena' (p.12).

Late Heidegger's 'language is the house of Being' and ethos = 'abode/dwelling place' (Letter on Humanism 1946) presupposes the 1924 framing in GA 18.108 ('Rhetorike peithous demiourgos: das Redenkonnen ist diejenige Moglichkeit, in der ich uber die Uberzeugung der Menschen, wie sie miteinander sind, die eigentliche Herrschaft habe').

P5 (pathos as Naturwissenschaft/Geisteswissenschaft transfer point) supports P10 (eidos of pathe as Being-in-the-world): if pathos is cosmologically primary, then the pathe of Aristotle Rhetoric II are properly read as ontological-dispositional rather than psychological/material. P10 is P5 specified at the human-rhetorical level.

Antihumanism (Derrida, Foucault, Bourdieu, Pecora et al.) takes Heidegger's middle voice as exemplifying agency-dissolution; Gross's P7 rejects this exemplification — the middle voice does not exemplify antihumanism but rather neo-Aristotelian protocommunitarianism.

P1 (SS 1924 as formative for BT) supports P10 (eidos of pathe as Being-in-the-world) genealogically: the rhetorical genealogy of BT key terms requires that the 1924 pathos-analysis be the source of BT's *Befindlichkeit* / *Furcht* (BT §§29-30).
